Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of refueling stops needed to reach target with given start fuel and station capacities.
Idea: Sweep stations in position order and use a max-heap of fuel from previously reachable stations.
Technique and why it applies: When current fuel cannot reach the next station, refuel from the largest available capacity, minimizing the number of stops for the range gained.
Invariant: The heap contains negated capacities of stations already passed but not yet chosen.
Edge cases: stations is mutated by appending the target with infinite capacity. Correctness assumes stations are sorted by location; otherwise the sweep order is invalid.
Complexity: For sorted stations, each heap operation is O(log n), giving O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence in a strictly increasing array.
Idea: Use pair states dp[j,k] and look for the predecessor value A[k]-A[j].
Technique and why it applies: A Fibonacci-like sequence is determined by its last two values. If the required predecessor occurs before j, its best length extends by one.
Invariant: dp[j,k] stores the longest valid sequence ending with A[j], A[k], with default length two.
Edge cases: collections is used without import. The method returns zero when no sequence of length at least three is found.
Complexity: The nested pair loops are O(n²) expected time and the pair-state map uses O(n²) space, not the author's stated O(n log M) space.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence of a strictly increasing array.
Idea: Try each pair as the first two values and repeatedly extend while the next sum exists in a set.
Technique and why it applies: Set membership checks whether each required next Fibonacci value appears anywhere in A. The sequence length increases for every successful extension.
Invariant: x and y are the latest two values in the candidate sequence, and l is its length.
Edge cases: The array is assumed strictly increasing and values are distinct. If no sequence reaches length three, the method returns zero rather than two.
Complexity: The nested pair loops plus extension search take O(n² log M) expected in common bounds, with O(n) set space.

Task and constraints: Simulate a robot moving on an unbounded grid, avoiding obstacles and maximizing squared distance from the origin.
Idea: Track position and orientation, turning on commands and stepping forward until blocked.
Technique and why it applies: The direction map converts orientation into a unit displacement. Each attempted step checks the obstacle set before changing coordinates.
Invariant: x,y represent the current unblocked position and a stores orientation in degrees.
Edge cases: Obstacles are stored as tuples for constant-time membership. The code updates the maximum only after a forward command, which is sufficient because turns do not change position.
Complexity: Runtime is O(total commanded steps + obstacle count) expected, with O(obstacles) storage.

Task and constraints: Simulate robot commands and return the greatest squared distance from the origin while avoiding obstacles.
Idea: Represent orientation as an index into four cardinal directions and move one step at a time.
Technique and why it applies: Turns adjust the direction index modulo four. Each step is taken only if the next coordinate is not in the obstacle set.
Invariant: x,y is the robot's current position and i identifies its heading.
Edge cases: An obstacle directly ahead stops the current command but does not stop later commands. The squared distance is updated after every successful step.
Complexity: Each attempted movement is checked once, giving O(total commanded steps + obstacle count) expected time and O(obstacles) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum integer eating speed that finishes all banana piles within h hours.
Idea: Binary-search speed between one and the largest pile.
Technique and why it applies: Required hours are the sum of ceiling(pile/speed), a non-increasing function of speed. Feasible speeds move the upper bound down; infeasible speeds move the lower bound up.
Invariant: The minimum feasible speed remains in the interval [l,r].
Edge cases: ceil is used without import in the snippet, so it requires an external definition. Piles are assumed nonempty and h is feasible.
Complexity: Each feasibility test scans n piles, and binary search takes O(log maxPile) tests, giving O(n log maxPile) time and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Determine the minimum eating speed that finishes all piles within H hours.
Idea: Binary-search K and test the total hours using integer ceiling division.
Technique and why it applies: (pile-1)//K+1 equals the ceiling of pile/K for positive piles, avoiding floating-point arithmetic.
Invariant: left is the smallest speed not yet ruled out, and right is the largest candidate still under consideration.
Edge cases: Empty piles would fail at max(piles), but the problem supplies at least one pile. The search returns left after the interval crosses.
Complexity: Each test is O(n), and O(log maxPile) tests give O(n log maxPile) time with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player wins the Stone Game when both players take a pile from either end.
Idea: Return True directly, relying on the theorem that the first player always wins for an even number of positive piles.
Technique and why it applies: With an even number of piles, the first player can choose all piles of one index parity and force a larger total than the opponent.
Invariant: No game state is calculated; the method encodes the guaranteed outcome for the problem's constraints.
Edge cases: The implementation also returns True for empty and odd-length inputs, although the standard problem guarantees an even number of piles. Under those broader inputs, the constant answer is not justified.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Decide whether Alice wins the end-picking Stone Game.
Idea: Use interval dynamic programming to compute the best score difference the current player can force.
Technique and why it applies: dp[j] stores the optimal difference for an interval ending at j; choosing either endpoint subtracts the opponent's best difference on the remaining interval.
Invariant: After each outer iteration, dp entries represent optimal score differences for intervals beginning at the current i.
Edge cases: The function returns True immediately for even-length inputs and length one. The standard problem guarantees an even number of piles, so the DP branch is normally unnecessary.
Complexity: The DP is O(n²) time and O(n) space when executed, but the early return covers all standard even-length inputs.

Task and constraints: Find the Nth positive integer divisible by A or B, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Binary-search the smallest number whose count of multiples of A or B is at least N.
Technique and why it applies: Inclusion-exclusion counts multiples as mid//A + mid//B - mid//lcm, removing double-counted common multiples.
Invariant: The search narrows to the first value with at least N magical numbers not exceeding it.
Edge cases: The fixed upper bound 10^14 may be insufficient for larger constraints. The final result applies modulo after finding the unmodded integer.
Complexity: Each test is O(1) after LCM calculation, so time is O(log bound) and space O(1).

Task and constraints: Return the Nth positive integer divisible by A or B, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Binary-search a numeric interval using a count of multiples of A or B.
Technique and why it applies: Inclusion-exclusion subtracts multiples of the LCM counted twice. The first value with count at least N is the desired magical number.
Invariant: left and right bracket the minimum number whose magical count reaches N.
Edge cases: The lower bound is min(A,B), which is a valid first candidate. The gcd helper uses Euclid's algorithm and assumes positive A and B.
Complexity: LCM calculation takes O(log min(A,B)); binary search uses O(log(max(A,B)N)) constant-time checks.

Task and constraints: Count subsets of crimes that use at most n members and earn at least minProfit, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Use a three-dimensional DP indexed by available people, required profit, and the next crime index.
Technique and why it applies: Each crime can be skipped or included if enough people are available. Profit is capped at the threshold using max(x-profit[j],0), merging all sufficiently profitable outcomes.
Invariant: arr[i][x][j] counts valid schemes using crimes j onward, with i people available and at least x profit still needed.
Edge cases: The base initialization makes zero remaining profit count as one scheme for each capacity. Memory grows quickly with all three dimensions.
Complexity: Time is O(n·minProfit·k) and space is O(n·minProfit·k).

Task and constraints: Count crime subsets using at most G members and at least P profit.
Idea: Maintain a two-dimensional DP by capped profit and used group size, updating in reverse for each crime.
Technique and why it applies: Each crime contributes its group and profit to prior states. Reversing both dimensions prevents the same crime from being selected more than once in the same iteration.
Invariant: dp[p][g] counts subsets using g members and profit capped at p after the crimes processed so far.
Edge cases: The code imports itertools but does not use it. It updates counts without reducing modulo until the final sum, so intermediate integers may become large.
Complexity: O(k·P·G) time and O(PG) space.

Task and constraints: Return the Kth character in a decoded string formed by letters and repetition digits, without materializing the full expansion.
Idea: Track accumulated lengths and repetition factors, then work backward through those lengths to map K to an original letter.
Technique and why it applies: Repetition divides the target index by the prior decoded length. If the reduced zero-based index corresponds to a stored letter position, that character is returned.
Invariant: acclens records decoded lengths at repetition boundaries, while idx maps selected expanded positions to source indices.
Edge cases: The appended '1' forces the final run to be recorded. The algorithm returns None if no index matches, despite the comment that this should never occur; correctness depends on its position bookkeeping.
Complexity: It uses O(n) preprocessing and O(n) reverse traversal, with O(n) auxiliary storage.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of boats needed to carry people, with each boat holding at most two people and total weight within limit.
Idea: Sort weights and pair the lightest remaining person with the heaviest whenever they fit.
Technique and why it applies: If the lightest cannot fit with the heaviest, the heaviest must ride alone; otherwise pairing them uses one boat and removes both extremes.
Invariant: lo and hi delimit the people not yet assigned to a boat.
Edge cases: people is sorted in place. Empty input returns zero because the loop never executes.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n) and the two-pointer scan is O(n), with O(1) auxiliary space beyond sorting.

Task and constraints: Minimize boats needed to transport everyone with at most two people per boat.
Idea: Sort people and greedily pair the lightest with the heaviest if they fit.
Technique and why it applies: The heaviest person must be assigned now. If the lightest fits with them, pair them; otherwise send the heaviest alone. Either way, one boat is used.
Invariant: left and right identify the lightest and heaviest unassigned people.
Edge cases: The method sorts people in place. A single remaining person receives one boat, and empty input returns zero.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting plus O(n) scan, with O(1) auxiliary space beyond sorting.

Task and constraints: Count original and subdivided nodes reachable from node zero using at most maxMoves edges.
Idea: Use Dijkstra to find shortest distances to original nodes and track how many subdivisions are reachable from each end of an edge.
Technique and why it applies: A path to a neighbor consumes one move per original edge plus its subdivisions. The remaining move budget determines the reachable portion of each subdivided edge.
Invariant: vis contains finalized original nodes; edgeofl tracks how much of a directed edge has been counted from that side.
Edge cases: defaultdict and heappush/heappop are used without imports. The strict condition p < maxMoves-cost can exclude an endpoint exactly at the budget boundary, so correctness needs scrutiny.
Complexity: Intended Dijkstra is O((V+E)log V), with O(V+E) storage.

Task and constraints: Count reachable original and subdivided nodes within M moves from node zero.
Idea: Run Dijkstra over original nodes and record how many subdivided nodes can be reached from each endpoint of every edge.
Technique and why it applies: best gives shortest distances. For an edge with w subdivisions, the two endpoint budgets cover min(w,remaining moves) nodes; their sum is capped at w to avoid double counting.
Invariant: count[u][v] records the reachable subdivision count from u toward v, capped by edge length.
Edge cases: Stale heap entries are skipped. Each original node is counted only when its best distance is popped, and edge contributions are added afterward.
Complexity: Dijkstra and edge accounting take O((V+E)log V) time and O(V+E) space.

Task and constraints: Compute the total projection area of a grid of stacked cubes onto the three coordinate planes.
Idea: Count nonzero cells for the top view and add each row and column maximum for the side views.
Technique and why it applies: Every nonempty stack contributes one unit to the top projection. Row maxima and column maxima give the projected heights in the other two views.
Invariant: result accumulates top-view occupied cells and the two side-view maximum sums.
Edge cases: The inner loop uses len(grid) for columns, assuming a square grid. Rectangular grids may be indexed incorrectly; the problem typically supplies a square matrix.
Complexity: For an N-by-N grid, time is O(N²) and auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return words that appear exactly once across two sentences combined.
Idea: Count all whitespace-separated words from both sentences and collect those with frequency one.
Technique and why it applies: Counter aggregates occurrences across both inputs, so a word present once in total is uncommon.
Invariant: x maps each word to its total frequency in s1 and s2.
Edge cases: Word comparison is case-sensitive and punctuation is retained as part of tokens. Output follows dictionary insertion order, which is not otherwise important to the result.
Complexity: Tokenization and counting take O(T) time and O(U) space for total text length T and distinct words U.
